Issued at 230 PM CDT Wed Jul 22 2026

Northwesterly flow is found over the northern Plains, situated 
as we are between a building upper level ridge to our west and a
Hudson Bay low to the northeast. Despite this pattern, dry 
conditions throughout lower to mid levels will greatly limit the
potential for notable precpitation or storms this afternoon and
evening, though we can never completely rule out isolated, 
diurnally driven light showers or weak storms this time of year.
Lingering smoke remains evident on satellite imagery across 
portions of northwestern and central North Dakota this 
afternoon, with steeper lapse rates allowing for at least some 
of this smoke to mix down to the surface, though this is 
expected to begin diminishing as light surface winds turns 
increasingly to the south-southwest this evening and overnight. 
Otherwise for today, near normal high temperatures in the lower 
to mid 80s are expected this afternoon as remain on the cool 
side of the ridge, while overnight lows are forecast in the mid 
50s to lower 60s. 

As we head into the later half of the week, the increasing 
influence of the upper level ridge as it attempts to build in 
across the Great Plains is going to allow for a warming trend 
that will again see well above normal high temperatures across 
western and central North Dakota this weekend. For Thursday, 
this influence is expected to be somewhat stymied by a weak 
shortwave riding along the ridge in the afternoon and evening, 
keeping forecast high temperatures mainly in the upper 80s to 
mid 90s range. Some limited instability (model values approx 
500-1000 J/KG along the International Border) and the favorable 
positioning of the upper level jet along with this weak wave 
will be sufficient to get some at least isolated thunderstorms 
across portions of the northwest and north central North Dakota 
Thursday afternoon and evening, though severe weather is not 
anticipated at the time of this forecast. 

A more robust convective environment is then anticipated across
portions of western and central North Dakota on Friday. With 
widespread high temperatures peaking into lower 90s to lower 
100s, and with dewpoints rising well into the mid to upper 60s 
across potions of the north central, model MUCAPE values Friday 
afternoon are beginning to rising into the 2500-3500 J/KG range.
Model bulk shear values around this time also begin to peak 
into into the 35 to 45 knots. There are a few things to consider
regarding location and coverage relating to possible convection
on Friday. Overall forcing during this period is relatively 
weak, and the greatest height rises are currently progged to be 
further south of the best convective environment up in the north
central, so it remains uncertain where there will be enough 
overlap to get things going. That being said, convective temps 
only in the lower to mid 90s and a developing low level jet in 
the north central may be sufficient to see some CI in the late 
afternoon and evening. Another point of contention is potential 
storm mode. Global models hint at a weak cold front / surface 
trough moving through the area Friday afternoon, roughly 
orientated in a SSW to NNE direction between the south central 
up through the Grand Forks area. With bulk shear vectors roughly
at at around 45 degree angle or less to this potential 
boundary, any storms that develop here may be more of a mixed 
storm mode. All of that is to say that advertising potential 
hazards is a little bit of a shamble. My current feeling is the 
primary hazard with any strong to severe storm is going to be 
damaging wind, as high DCAPE values around 1000- 1500 J/KG 
expected, and high lapse rates around 9.0-10.0 C/km will allow 
some of the stronger winds from the jet to mix down toward the 
surface, and as the dry, inverted-v signature on model soundings
hint at the potential downward acceleration due to evaporative 
processes. Otherwise, the potential for large hail is also 
there, especially if any discrete, surface-based storms manages 
to poke through the residual CIN lingering across the area. The 
highest hail threat would be associated with any supercells that
manage to develop, as hinted by sufficient 0-6KM shear values 
and the modest clockwise elongation of the hodographs evident 
across portions of the north central, include the northern James
River Valley. As it stands, the SPC has placed portions of 
central North Dakota into a Marginal (Level 1 of 5) risk for 
isolated severe thunderstorms for Friday. 

Otherwise, the main point of concern Friday heading into the 
weekend is going to be the very hot temperatures. High 
temperatures each day are expected to peak into the 100-105 
degree range, with such temperatures expected to be fairly 
widespread on Saturday and Sunday. Overall moisture availability
will be a little lower than last week's heat event, which is 
expected to keep apparent temperatures generally in criteria for
a Heat Advisory
